chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
Nokia Corporation — headquartered in Espoo, Finland, listed primarily on HEX:NOKIA and trading as an American Depositary Receipt on the NYSE under the ticker NOK — entered 2025 carrying two corporate facts that together constituted a strategic inflection. On February 28, 2025, Nokia completed its acquisition of [Infinera Corporation](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-completes-acquisition-of-infinera-to-create-innovation-powerhouse-in-optical-networks-with-the-scale-to-power-the-data-center-revolution/) for approximately $2.3 billion (~€2.1 billion), a deal announced the previous June that substantially scaled its Optical Networks business and deepened existing relationships with North American hyperscalers. Thirty days later, on April 1, 2025, Justin Hotard — formerly Executive Vice President and General Manager of the Data Center and AI Group at Intel Corporation — succeeded Pekka Lundmark as President and Chief Executive Officer. Together, those two events pushed a company best known for radio access network equipment and the routing legacy of its 2016 Alcatel-Lucent acquisition toward a market the new chief executive had already named the AI supercycle.

## The Succession and Its Rationale

Hotard's career profile was calibrated for the moment. Before Intel he had been EVP and General Manager of the High Performance Computing and AI Business at Hewlett Packard Enterprise, accumulating more than a decade operating in the compute, accelerator, and data-centre infrastructure markets that Nokia was now reorienting to serve. The Iowa State University industrial engineering graduate and Northwestern Kellogg MBA holder was Nokia's most explicit signal of strategic intent. Board chair Sari Baldauf stated the hire plainly:

> "He has a strong track record of accelerating growth in technology companies along with vast expertise in AI and data center markets."

Hotard's opening formulation of Nokia's positioning drew directly on the vantage point he had occupied at Intel:

> "Networking comes second only to compute hardware when it comes to share of AI datacenter investment."

And, in a framing that would recur through subsequent quarters:

> "We're at the start of a super cycle with AI — very similar to the one we saw a couple of decades ago with the internet."

## Four Business Groups

Nokia at succession operated across four business groups. Network Infrastructure — led by Federico Guillen — comprised IP Networks (the Alcatel-Lucent-heritage routing franchise, including the SR Linux operating system being positioned for AI data-centre fabric deployments), Optical Networks (substantially enlarged by Infinera), Fixed Networks, and Submarine Networks. Mobile Networks, led by Tommi Uitto, housed the 5G radio access network business that had historically anchored Nokia's revenues. Cloud and Network Services delivered software and managed services. Nokia Technologies, led by Jenni Lukander, monetised the company's patent portfolio — a high-margin recurring stream spanning mobile communications, multimedia, and IoT licensing.

The four-group structure was itself scheduled for rationalisation. In mid-2025, Nokia announced a simplification into two reporting segments — Network Infrastructure and Mobile Infrastructure — effective January 1, 2026, alongside a strategy revamp that targeted comparable operating profit of EUR 2.7 billion to EUR 3.2 billion (~$2.9–$3.4 billion) by 2028, and five strategic priorities centred on AI, cloud, and next-generation mobile. [Nokia Strategy 2025](https://telecomlead.com/telecom-equipment/nokia-strategy-2025-ten-key-targets-to-lead-the-ai-driven-network-era-123541)

## Revenue Backdrop

The financial context against which Hotard assumed command was one of contraction off a 2022 peak. Full-year 2024 revenue came in at approximately EUR 19.7 billion (~$21.0 billion), down from the EUR 24.9 billion summit of 2022 as carrier capital-expenditure cycles moderated following the initial 5G build-out wave.

| Year | Net Sales (EUR bn) |
|------|--------------------|
| 2020 | 21.9 |
| 2021 | 22.2 |
| 2022 | 24.9 |
| 2023 | 22.3 |
| 2024 | ~19.7 |

In Q1 2025 — the first full quarter absorbing Infinera — Nokia reported consolidated net sales of approximately EUR 4.39 billion (~$4.7 billion), with Network Infrastructure growing 11 per cent on a constant-currency basis. IP Networks contributed EUR 646 million (~$693 million) of that segment's revenue. A one-time EUR 120 million contract settlement charge in Mobile Networks produced a group net loss of EUR 60 million for the period; the underlying operating trajectory was characterised as stabilising. [Nokia Q1 2025 Interim Report](https://capyfin.com/s/nyse/NOK/q1-2025-earnings-report)

## Infinera Integration and Optical Scale

Infinera brought a US-based photonic integrated circuit design capability, a Latin American carrier customer base, and — critically — hyperscaler relationships Nokia's legacy optical business had not cultivated at the same depth. By Q1 2025 the enlarged Optical Networks unit was posting 15 per cent net-sales growth year-on-year. By Q2, book-to-bill was described as well above one, driven by new hyperscaler orders including a first award for 800G pluggables from a major US hyperscaler. Management subsequently characterised integration as proceeding ahead of plan, and by the close of 2025 Nokia was claiming the number-one position in optical market share globally — a competitive claim implausible before the Infinera close. [Nokia doubles down on optical and AI-era connectivity, Capacity](https://capacityglobal.com/news/nokia-manish-gulyani-interview/)

## IP Networks and the NVIDIA Signal

In parallel, Nokia's IP Networks unit was advancing SR Linux — the open, programmable network operating system built on the Alcatel-Lucent routing heritage — as the platform for AI data-centre fabric deployments. In May 2025, Nokia and Supermicro announced a joint solution combining Supermicro's 800G Ethernet switching hardware with SR Linux and Nokia's Event-Driven Automation platform, targeting hyperscaler and cloud-provider deployments at scale. [Nokia–Supermicro partnership](https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-and-supermicro-partner-to-deliver-integrated-ai-optimized-data-center-networking-solutions/)

The competitive signal sharpened in October 2025: NVIDIA announced a USD 1.0 billion (~€0.93 billion) equity investment in Nokia at $6.01 per share, making the GPU company a 2.90 per cent Nokia shareholder, coupled with a strategic partnership to develop AI-RAN products for 5G-Advanced and 6G using NVIDIA's Aerial RAN Compute Pro platform, with T-Mobile field trials scheduled to begin in 2026. [NVIDIA Newsroom](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-nokia-ai-telecommunications) Hotard's statement on the partnership extended well beyond a single product line:

> "The next leap in telecom isn't just from 5G to 6G — it's a fundamental redesign of the network to deliver AI-powered connectivity, capable of processing intelligence from the data center all the way to the edge."

## Open Questions

As of the dossier's frozen snapshot in May 2026, the strategic repositioning is substantive in direction but early in revenue delivery. The questions this dossier pursues are three: whether Hotard's AI data-centre operating depth translates into measurable IP Networks routing revenue at hyperscaler customers — against switching-native competitors Cisco Systems, Juniper Networks, and Arista Networks that hold far deeper data-centre incumbent positions; whether the Infinera integration delivers the cost synergies and hyperscaler-footprint expansion that management has projected at the scale required to justify the EUR 2.1 billion outlay; and whether the NVIDIA partnership produces commercial AI-RAN revenue or remains primarily a balance-sheet endorsement. Nokia's Mobile Networks franchise — competitively matched against Ericsson and Samsung Networks across the global 5G market, with indirect upside from western-market Huawei restrictions — provides the earnings base from which the AI infrastructure bet must be funded. The strategy is articulated; the execution is the chapter that follows.

chapters.title: From 1865 Finnish founding through Alcatel-Lucent, Lundmark, Infinera, and Hotard
chapters.body:
## The Finnish Conglomerate, 1865–1990

Nokia Corporation's origins bear almost no resemblance to the telecommunications equipment vendor it became. On 12 May 1865, a Finnish mining engineer named Fredrik Idestam established a wood-pulp mill on the banks of the Tammerkoski rapids near Tampere, south-western Finland. A second mill followed two years later on the Nokia River, close to the small town of Nokia — a name derived, in the local dialect, from a dark-furred riverbank animal. The company incorporated formally under the Nokia name in 1871. For most of the nineteenth century, its business was paper.

The twentieth century transformed it into something more complex. A series of mergers across rubber manufacturing — Finnish Rubber Works joined the group in 1922 — and cable production — Finnish Cable Works in 1967 — produced a diversified industrial conglomerate operating across tyres, consumer footwear, consumer electronics, and telecommunications cables. The three-company structure formalised as Nokia Corporation in 1967. By the 1980s the group had moved into mobile telecommunications in earnest, supplying analogue network equipment and, from 1987, handsets for the Nordic Mobile Telephone standard. Finland's cold, dispersed geography provided the demand logic. Nokia was a conglomerate learning, improbably, to become a technology company.

## The Mobile Phone Era and Its End

The 1990s produced the most dramatic transformation in Nokia's history. The company divested its non-core industrial businesses — rubber, cables, consumer electronics — and concentrated almost entirely on mobile handsets and network infrastructure. The timing proved extraordinarily fortunate. Global mobile adoption accelerated through the decade, and Nokia captured the wave. By the early 2000s the company commanded roughly a third to forty percent of the global handset market, making it the most valuable company in Europe by market capitalisation at its peak. Espoo had replaced Detroit and Stuttgart as a symbol of industrial dominance.

The collapse arrived with the iPhone. Apple's entry into smartphones in 2007, followed by Google's Android platform in 2008, exposed Nokia's Symbian software stack as inadequate for the new computing paradigm. Nokia's response — the Symbian defence, the belated Microsoft Windows Phone partnership announced in February 2011 under incoming CEO Stephen Elop — failed to arrest the decline. Market share collapsed from above forty percent to single digits within five years. The handset business that had defined the company for two decades became unsustainable.

In September 2013, Nokia's board agreed to sell the Devices and Services division to Microsoft Corporation for €5.44 billion (approximately $7.2 billion). The transaction completed in April 2014. What remained was a smaller, structurally different entity: Nokia Solutions and Networks, the telecommunications infrastructure business, plus Nokia Technologies, the patent licensing operation. The handset era was over. The network infrastructure era was beginning.

## The Alcatel-Lucent Acquisition, January 2016

The strategic direction clarified in April 2015, when Nokia announced an agreement to acquire Alcatel-Lucent, the Franco-American telecommunications equipment vendor that carried the heritage of AT&T's Bell Laboratories. The transaction valued Alcatel-Lucent at approximately €15.6 billion (roughly $15.6 billion at prevailing exchange rates) and closed in [January 2016](https://www.nokia.com/investors/), creating a substantially larger network infrastructure company capable of competing with Ericsson, Huawei, and Cisco across a broader product range.

The Alcatel-Lucent acquisition brought three capabilities that would prove foundational to the subsequent decade. First, it delivered IP Networks routing — specifically the 7750 Service Router platform and the broader IP/MPLS networking portfolio — which established Nokia in carrier routing alongside Cisco and Juniper. Second, it added a coherent optical transport portfolio through Alcatel-Lucent's Wavelength Division Multiplexing business. Third, it transferred the Bell Laboratories research lineage and the accompanying US government, enterprise, and hyperscaler customer relationships that Alcatel-Lucent had cultivated across decades. Nokia paid a substantial premium for a struggling asset; it acquired capabilities whose strategic value would compound across the following decade in ways not immediately apparent at close.

CEO Rajeev Suri, who led Nokia from 2014 through 2020, oversaw the integration and used the enlarged platform to position Nokia as a primary 5G infrastructure vendor. The 5G cycle produced a revenue expansion that peaked at €24.9 billion in 2022 before a sharp deceleration as carrier capital expenditure moderated globally.

## The Lundmark Era: 2020–2025

Pekka Lundmark succeeded Suri as chief executive in August 2020, inheriting a company that had grown rapidly but whose cost structure had not kept pace with the strategic transformation. Lundmark, a Finnish engineer who had previously run Fortum, the state-controlled energy company, and earlier held senior roles at Nokia and Kone, moved quickly to restructure.

The Lundmark programme had three principal dimensions. Organisational simplification first: Nokia consolidated around four business groups — Network Infrastructure, Mobile Networks, Cloud and Network Services, and Nokia Technologies — creating clearer profit-and-loss accountability. Cost reduction second: a restructuring programme targeting approximately €600 million in annual savings reduced headcount and rationalised the engineering footprint across multiple geographies. Strategic repositioning third: Lundmark consistently framed Nokia as a network infrastructure pure-play, differentiating it from Ericsson's mobile-dominated revenue mix and from Cisco's software-heavy positioning.

Revenue through the Lundmark period fell from the €24.9 billion 2022 peak to €19.7 billion in 2024 as carrier spending softened — a trajectory detailed in the Snapshot chapter. The compression concentrated strategic attention on Network Infrastructure, where the Alcatel-Lucent-inherited IP routing and optical transport capabilities offered structural diversification away from mobile carrier spending cycles — a secular exposure Nokia's board had recognised as a long-term vulnerability.

## The Infinera Acquisition, 2024–2025

In June 2024, Nokia announced the acquisition of Infinera Corporation, a US-based optical transport equipment vendor listed on the Nasdaq, for approximately $2.3 billion in a cash-and-stock transaction. The strategic logic was explicit and multi-dimensional.

Infinera contributed a coherent optical transport product line anchored by the ICE (Infinite Capacity Engine) digital signal processor chipset, which had earned a position among hyperscaler and data centre interconnect customers seeking high-capacity, programmable optical transport. Critically, Infinera brought a US-anchored customer base that skewed toward technology companies, cloud providers, and Latin American carriers — categories that complemented Nokia's existing telecommunications relationships and provided exposure to hyperscaler capital expenditure cycles increasingly dominated by AI infrastructure deployment. The acquisition also provided US manufacturing presence and US-based engineering design capability relevant to evolving supply chain requirements and the increasing sensitivity of US government and enterprise customers to vendor provenance.

The transaction received regulatory approvals and closed on February 28, 2025. The combined Optical Networks segment — incorporating the legacy Nokia portfolio and the Infinera assets — emerged as a substantially larger participant in data centre interconnect and long-haul optical infrastructure, positioned precisely as hyperscaler spending on AI training and inference clusters was accelerating the demand for high-bandwidth optical connectivity between facilities.

## The Hotard Succession, April 2025

Justin Hotard assumed the presidency and chief executive role on April 1, 2025, succeeding Lundmark. The board's selection telegraphed a strategic direction the company had been building toward since the Alcatel-Lucent integration: Nokia's SR Linux network operating system had been gaining traction in AI data centre fabric applications, and Hotard's Intel and HPE data-centre background positioned him to accelerate that pivot.

The company that began as a paper mill on the Nokia River in 1865, that briefly led the world in mobile handsets, and that acquired the Bell Laboratories heritage in January 2016, was entering its latest strategic chapter under its newest chief executive: a European-listed network infrastructure vendor with American leadership, seeking to position Alcatel-Lucent's inherited routing capability and Infinera's freshly integrated optical transport assets at the centre of the most capital-intensive infrastructure build-out of the AI era.

chapters.title: Network Infrastructure, Mobile Networks, Cloud and Network Services, Nokia Technologies
chapters.body:
## Four Groups, One Strategic Pivot

Nokia entered 2025 operating through four reportable business groups — Network Infrastructure, Mobile Networks, Cloud and Network Services, and Nokia Technologies. Two of those groups, Network Infrastructure and Nokia Technologies, carried the highest margin profiles and the most direct exposure to hyperscaler demand — positioning them at the centre of CEO Justin Hotard's AI data-centre pivot.

## Network Infrastructure: The Commercial Engine

Network Infrastructure was Nokia's largest group by segment contribution, encompassing four distinct sub-businesses — IP Networks, Optical Networks, Fixed Networks, and Submarine Networks — that together carried the bulk of Nokia's non-mobile revenue and the most strategically freighted asset in the portfolio.

**IP Networks** sat at the centre of the new strategic narrative. The portfolio traced directly to Alcatel-Lucent's Service Router Operating System heritage, and Nokia had developed SR Linux — a modern, open, containerised network operating system built for cloud-scale deployments — as the platform for its 7250 IXR (Internet Exchange Router) series. Where legacy routers were designed for telco service chaining, the 7250 IXR was architected for the leaf-and-spine topologies that hyperscalers deploy inside their data centres, and for the AI data centre's particular demand: high-bandwidth, low-latency switching across dense GPU clusters. The underlying Nokia FP5 network processor delivered 800-gigabit Ethernet port density and the forwarding throughput required for scale-out AI training fabrics.

Nokia had not disclosed a discrete AI data-centre routing revenue target by the frozen snapshot date, but Microsoft's engagement with Nokia's IP routing for AI data-centre fabric — noted in the Snapshot chapter — validated the strategic framing.

**Optical Networks** was materially larger after the Infinera close. Infinera brought its ICE6 and ICE-X coherent DSP technology, the GX series of optical transport platforms, and a customer book weighted toward North American carriers and Latin American operators — geographies where Nokia's legacy optical footprint had been thinner. The combined optical business competed against [Ciena](https://www.ciena.com), Cisco's optical division (incorporating the former Acacia coherent silicon acquisition), and Huawei's optical arm. The integration thesis rested on scale: in silicon R&D cost amortisation, in combined customer breadth across the Atlantic, and in the ability to offer an end-to-end transport solution from long-haul submarine routes to metro access rings.

**Fixed Networks** encompassed Nokia's broadband access portfolio — GPON and XGS-PON passive optical network equipment and digital subscriber line technology — sold primarily to incumbent carriers deploying fibre-to-the-home. Government-funded broadband programmes in the United States (the BEAD initiative), the United Kingdom, and across the European Union provided a multi-year secular tailwind, though Nokia competed here against Calix, Huawei, and ZTE. The segment was not a growth driver in the AI data-centre narrative, but it provided durable, if modest, volume.

**Submarine Networks** operated as a comparatively small but strategically useful business, building and maintaining long-haul undersea cable systems. Hyperscaler-funded transoceanic cable investment — with Google, Microsoft, Meta, and Amazon all commissioning dedicated capacity on privately owned routes — provided demand less correlated with carrier capital cycles than the rest of Nokia's revenue. Nokia competed in this segment against [SubCom](https://www.subcom.com) and Alcatel Submarine Networks (ASN), the latter a former sister division from the Alcatel-Lucent era now owned by Draka/Prysmian.

## Mobile Networks: 5G Maturity and Market Position

Mobile Networks remained a substantial contributor by absolute revenue, though the segment had borne the sharpest contraction during the 2023–2024 carrier spending correction. The global 5G radio access network market operated as an effective three-vendor oligopoly among Nokia, Ericsson, and Huawei, with Samsung Networks pressing to extend beyond its Korean and North American strongholds.

Nokia's AirScale RAN platform — incorporating the company's ReefShark system-on-chip family — underpinned deployments across Tier 1 operators in North America, Europe, and India. AT&T, Verizon, Deutsche Telekom, and major Indian carriers held active Nokia RAN relationships. The competitive dynamic with Ericsson was persistent: both vendors tendered on the same contracts, competed on total cost of ownership, and differentiated primarily on software capability and integration services. Samsung was a more acute threat in specific geographies, particularly Japan and deployments aligned with Open RAN specifications.

Huawei restrictions introduced by the United States, the United Kingdom, Sweden, and a growing list of governments from 2019 onward created displacement opportunities that Nokia and Ericsson shared. The UK's requirement that Huawei equipment be removed from core networks by 2027, with access networks following on a longer timeline, translated into a multi-year re-equipment programme. The indirect upside was real but timing-extended; neither Nokia nor Ericsson could book the full Huawei displacement as incremental revenue in a single reporting period.

| Vendor | Est. 2024 Global RAN Share | Primary Geography |
|---|---|---|
| Huawei | ~30% | China, Middle East, Africa, parts of Europe |
| Ericsson | ~25% | North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific |
| Nokia | ~22% | North America, Europe, India |
| Samsung | ~12% | Korea, United States, Japan |
| ZTE and others | ~11% | Emerging markets |

The transition to Open RAN — disaggregated radio hardware and software — remained slower than proponents had forecast by the mid-2020s. Nokia supported O-RAN Alliance specifications and offered a cloud-native RAN software stack, but the company preserved a substantial proprietary hardware business and showed no urgency to accelerate disaggregation faster than carrier procurement actually demanded.

## Cloud and Network Services: The Software Lever

Cloud and Network Services was the smallest of the four groups by revenue but carried strategic importance as Nokia's vehicle for recurring software and managed-services income. The portfolio encompassed OSS and BSS management software — used by operators to orchestrate network automation, customer management, and service fulfilment — alongside professional services, managed services, and systems integration engagements.

The group competed with Amdocs, Netcracker (NEC), Ericsson's digital services arm, and a range of IT services vendors on large carrier transformation programmes. Margins were structurally lower than IP Networks or Nokia Technologies, but revenue recurrence was higher than hardware. Under the efficiency programme that Pekka Lundmark initiated across 2023 and 2024 — which reduced Nokia's global headcount by roughly 16,000 positions — Cloud and Network Services was a primary target for margin improvement through platform consolidation and reduced duplication in professional services delivery.

Hotard's AI strategic posture intersected with this group: Nokia was positioning network automation software as a beneficiary of AI-assisted network management, offering operators tooling for predictive maintenance, automated configuration, and energy optimisation across increasingly complex multi-vendor network estates. Whether this represented a durable software revenue expansion or a marketing reframe of existing OSS capabilities remained to be demonstrated in bookings.

## Nokia Technologies: The High-Margin Franchise

Nokia Technologies generated revenue through licensing Nokia's intellectual property portfolio to device manufacturers, automotive companies, and consumer electronics vendors. The licensing model produced revenue estimated in the range of €1.3 billion to €1.5 billion annually at operating margins above 40 percent — providing revenue visibility unusual elsewhere in the portfolio and a financial buffer during hardware revenue cycle troughs.

## Segment Structure in Context

| Segment | Strategic Role | Margin Profile | Principal Competitors |
|---|---|---|---|
| Network Infrastructure | Hardware platform + AI data-centre pivot | Mid-teens operating margin | Cisco, Juniper, Arista, Ciena, Huawei |
| Mobile Networks | 5G RAN — volume revenue | High single-digit to low-teens | Ericsson, Samsung Networks, Huawei |
| Cloud and Network Services | Software and services recurring | Mid single-digit | Amdocs, Ericsson Digital, Netcracker |
| Nokia Technologies | Patent licensing | ~40%+ operating margin | N/A — licensing, not product competition |

Nokia's €19.7 billion 2024 revenue reflected the trough of the carrier spending correction that followed the 2022 5G peak. The Infinera acquisition, closed barely five weeks before Hotard formally took the chair, expanded the optical footprint at the precise moment hyperscaler demand for wavelength capacity was accelerating. The Microsoft IP routing engagement planted a flag in the AI data-centre router market that Cisco, Juniper, and Arista had long considered their own. Whether Nokia's historical strengths in carrier-grade reliability and standards-compliance could be repositioned as advantages in hyperscaler procurement — rather than liabilities in a market that prizes software programmability and commodity economics — was the central commercial question the new chief executive inherited on day one.

chapters.title: Revenue trajectory, segment economics, capital allocation
chapters.body:
Nokia's revenue arc across the five years to 2024 traces the anatomy of a telecommunications-equipment supercycle — the climb, the crest, and the correction — in stark numerical form. Understanding how that trajectory unfolded at the segment level, and how management deployed its balance sheet through the descent, is essential context for evaluating what Hotard's AI data centre pivot is actually working with.

## The Five-Year Revenue Arc

From a base of €21.9 billion in 2020, Nokia's net sales climbed modestly to €22.2 billion in 2021 as pandemic-delayed network investment resumed and early 5G deployments accelerated across North America and Europe. The cycle peaked sharply in 2022 at €24.9 billion — a figure that reflected simultaneous 5G ramp programmes at AT&T, Verizon, T-Mobile, and several large European operators, layered on top of solid demand in the IP Networks routing franchise and a government-stimulated broadband build-out across Fixed Networks. Nokia had not recorded revenue at that level since the feature-phone era.

The reversal was swift and unforgiving. By 2023 net sales had retreated to €22.3 billion as North American carriers, having front-loaded capital expenditure to complete C-band spectrum deployments, pulled back sharply on equipment orders. Nokia's Mobile Networks segment bore the heaviest volume impact; IP Networks and Fixed Networks proved somewhat more resilient, sustained by enterprise and government demand, but could not offset the wireless contraction. The decline extended into 2024, when net sales compressed a further €2.6 billion to approximately €19.7 billion — Nokia's weakest top-line performance in the post-Alcatel-Lucent era and a number that concentrated attention on what proportion of the lost revenue was structural rather than cyclical.

| Fiscal Year | Net Sales (€B) | YoY Change |
|---|---|---|
| 2020 | 21.9 | — |
| 2021 | 22.2 | +1.4% |
| 2022 | 24.9 | +12.2% |
| 2023 | 22.3 | –10.4% |
| 2024 | 19.7 | –11.7% |

*Source: [Nokia investor relations](https://www.nokia.com/investors/); prep data as of 2026-05-25.*

Cumulatively, Nokia surrendered €5.2 billion — approximately 21 percent — of peak-cycle revenue over two years. The compression was not uniform across the portfolio: Mobile Networks absorbed the bulk of the absolute volume decline, while the Network Infrastructure cluster (IP Networks, Optical Networks, Fixed Networks, Submarine Networks) demonstrated meaningful resilience, a dynamic that would subsequently shape Hotard's strategic repositioning toward AI data centre infrastructure.

## Segment Economics

Nokia reports through four business groups whose economics differ materially, making the top-line revenue trend a partial and sometimes misleading guide to underlying profitability.

**Mobile Networks** is the largest segment by revenue and the most cyclically exposed. It supplies 5G radio-access-network equipment and software to mobile operators worldwide, competing against Ericsson, Samsung Networks, and — where regulatory frameworks permit — Huawei. The business carries structurally thinner margins than the IP routing or patent licensing franchises, owing to the hardware intensity of RAN deployment and the necessity of sustained R&D investment to remain competitive in antenna design, baseband silicon, and cloud-native RAN software. At the 2022 peak, Mobile Networks generated outsized absolute operating profit on volume; through 2023 and 2024, the combination of volume contraction and pricing pressure from Ericsson and Samsung compressed the segment's contribution, making it the primary drag on group results and the principal source of analyst concern about Nokia's earnings quality.

**Network Infrastructure** groups IP Networks, Optical Networks, Fixed Networks, and Submarine Networks under a single reporting umbrella. The economics within the cluster vary significantly. IP Networks — the Alcatel-Lucent-heritage routing portfolio, centred today on the SR Linux platform — carries comparatively higher software content and has historically operated at margins above the group average. Submarine Networks can exhibit wide swings around major project deliveries. The Infinera integration, completed 28 February 2025, added scale in coherent optical components and dense-wavelength-division-multiplexing transmission, deepening Nokia's position with hyperscaler customers constructing private long-haul fibre networks to connect disaggregated AI data centre campuses — the infrastructure layer that Hotard identified as a strategic priority before his first quarterly earnings call.

**Cloud and Network Services** encompasses network-management software, private wireless enterprise 5G, and professional services. The segment's margin profile has historically trailed the hardware businesses in absolute terms, but it carries a more predictable recurring-revenue character as Nokia has shifted toward software subscriptions and multi-year managed-service contracts. The shift matters disproportionately in a down-cycle: CNS revenue proved less volatile than Mobile Networks through the 2023–2024 correction.

**Nokia Technologies** is the group's highest-margin business and its least capital-intensive. The unit licenses Nokia's accumulated patent estate — spanning wireless standards from 2G through 5G — to handset manufacturers, automotive companies, and consumer electronics producers on a global basis. Operating margins in Nokia Technologies have historically ranged above 50 percent and in stronger licensing cycles have approached 70–80 percent, making the unit a disproportionate contributor to group operating profit relative to its revenue share. The franchise does carry litigation and renewal risk: major handset-vendor licence renegotiations are periodic, occasionally contested, and can introduce lumpiness into the Nokia Technologies revenue line in the year of renegotiation.

The interplay between these four segments means Nokia's reported group operating margin is a composite of the high-margin Technologies business, the structurally attractive but comparatively small IP Networks franchise, and the high-volume but thinner-margin Mobile Networks operation. Analysts focused solely on top-line revenue trends systematically underweight the earnings-quality differential embedded in the segment mix.

## Capital Structure and Balance Sheet

Under Pekka Lundmark, Nokia undertook a material balance-sheet rehabilitation alongside its operational restructuring. The company had entered the Lundmark era — he succeeded Rajeev Suri in August 2020 — carrying residual integration liabilities from the Alcatel-Lucent transaction, including substantial defined-benefit pension obligations accumulated across the combined European entity. By the time Lundmark handed the keys to Hotard on 1 April 2025, Nokia carried a net-cash balance sheet, providing the financial flexibility to pursue the Infinera acquisition without approaching external debt markets on distressed terms during a period when its own equity was depressed by the carrier-spending correction.

The Infinera transaction — closed 28 February 2025 at approximately $2.3 billion — was structured to preserve Nokia's investment-grade credit profile. Management expected the acquisition to be accretive to EPS within the first full year, primarily through cost synergies and cross-selling of IP Networks routing into Infinera's hyperscaler relationships.

Research-and-development expenditure has remained a significant and remarkably stable charge. Nokia has historically invested in the range of 15–17 percent of net sales in R&D — a commitment that reflects the twin necessity of competing in the 5G RAN market, where the technology refresh cycle is compressed, and sustaining the patent portfolio that underpins Nokia Technologies licensing revenue. The absolute R&D spend declined alongside revenues through 2023 and 2024, but the proportional commitment was largely maintained. Neither Lundmark nor Hotard chose to harvest the R&D line to defend near-term profitability margins — a discipline that distinguishes Nokia's approach from some peers who have cut engineering spend during demand troughs and subsequently struggled with product competitiveness at cycle recovery.

## Share Repurchase and Capital Return

Nokia's capital-return programme accelerated materially during the latter Lundmark years as the balance sheet strengthened. The company executed a €600 million share-repurchase programme in tranches, conducted through market purchases on Nasdaq Helsinki and disclosed through the regulatory notification framework applicable to Finnish-listed issuers. The rationale management articulated was consistent with standard capital-allocation theory: Nokia's sum-of-the-parts value — combining the Nokia Technologies patent franchise, which commands earnings multiples well above those applied to telecommunications equipment businesses, with the Network Infrastructure and Mobile Networks assets — was not reflected in the prevailing market capitalisation during a period of cyclical earnings pressure.

By reducing the share count, Nokia improved earnings per share even in a period of declining absolute net income, and returned surplus capital to shareholders at a time when the dividend itself was being managed cautiously against the competing priority of preserving acquisition firepower. Nokia reinstated its ordinary dividend following the Alcatel-Lucent integration years and has subsequently maintained a progressive distribution policy, supplemented in select years by special dividends when free cash flow permitted. The Infinera acquisition absorbed capital that might otherwise have funded an accelerated buyback in 2025, deferring the next phase of the repurchase programme into the Hotard era.

The capital-allocation calculus under Hotard has shifted its centre of gravity. The AI data centre routing opportunity — centred on the SR Linux platform in IP Networks and the enlarged Optical Networks portfolio following Infinera consolidation — requires continued engineering investment and sales-force expansion into the hyperscaler account base rather than capital harvesting for shareholder return. Hotard, drawing explicitly on his Intel Data Center and AI background, has signalled a preference for reinvesting in the Network Infrastructure portfolio to capture what Nokia's management characterises as a generational infrastructure replacement cycle in AI data centre routing. Whether the financial model that emerges — Mobile Networks volumes recovering modestly as the carrier-spending cycle turns, IP Networks revenues accelerating into hyperscaler accounts, Infinera integration synergies materialising on the promised schedule — can lift Nokia back toward the €24.9 billion peak of 2022 remains, at the frozen snapshot date of 23 May 2026, the central empirical question of the Hotard tenure.

chapters.title: Post-Lundmark era through Infinera close and Hotard succession
chapters.body:
## The Revenue Compression That Forced a Reckoning

The revenue compression from €24.9 billion (2022) to €19.7 billion (2024) — detailed in the Financial chapter — was accompanied by a restructuring programme targeting approximately 14,000 role reductions and €800 million in cost savings by end-2026. [Nokia Investor Relations](https://www.nokia.com/investors/)

## Infinera and the Optical Bet

The Infinera close on February 28, 2025 added roughly 3,200 employees and positioned Nokia alongside Ciena as a primary supplier of data-centre-interconnect and long-haul transport infrastructure. Critically, Infinera's installed base skewed toward hyperscaler accounts — the customer segment Hotard would subsequently address with the IP Networks routing portfolio.

## The Succession and What It Signalled

Justin Hotard succeeded Lundmark as CEO effective April 1, 2025. The board's choice — an Intel data-centre executive rather than a telecom veteran — was a statement about where Nokia's forward growth opportunity sat.

## Hotard's Quarterly Cadence

Hotard's first full earnings cycle as CEO began with the Q1 2025 results, reported in late April 2025. The quarter incorporated the first contribution from the closed Infinera assets and established the baseline against which his AI data centre narrative would be measured. Management commentary from that call emphasised the complementarity between the IP Networks routing portfolio — the 7750 SR platform and the FP5 silicon generation — and the optical transport capability Infinera added, framing the combined offering as an end-to-end solution for the data-centre-interconnect and wide-area-network requirements of hyperscaler AI campuses.

Nokia's Network Infrastructure segment had been posting more resilient revenue trends than Mobile Networks through the 2023-2024 correction. The routing business, in particular, had benefited from the early stages of hyperscaler network refresh cycles driven by AI workload growth. Cloud and internet companies were building out spine-and-leaf fabrics and wide-area transport at a pace that offset some of the carrier capex pullback. The IP Networks routing portfolio, under the presidency of Federico Guillen's Network Infrastructure business group, was at the centre of that dynamic.

Hotard inherited a company whose Mobile Networks revenue base was substantially diminished from 5G-deployment-peak levels, and whose IP Networks and Optical Networks segments were being asked to provide the growth narrative that the carrier business could no longer supply.

## The AI Routing Thesis Meets Reality

The structural opportunity in AI data centre networking is not hypothetical. The shift to architectures supporting 400G, 800G, and eventually 1.6T interfaces for GPU cluster interconnect has created purchasing cycles where Nokia's FP5-based routing platforms compete directly with Cisco and Juniper.

Hotard's operating experience at Intel's Data Center and AI Group meant he had been a buyer and partner of exactly the networking infrastructure Nokia was now selling. That symmetry — understanding the hyperscaler procurement cycle from the inside — was the core rationale for the succession. CFO Marco Wirén, who had joined from Wärtsilä in January 2021 and navigated the multi-year restructuring with Lundmark, provided continuity on the financial execution side as Hotard established the new strategic posture.

The Infinera close, completed six weeks before Hotard's first day, was the enabling transaction. Without the optical transport depth that Infinera added to the Optical Networks segment, the AI data centre narrative would have been confined to routing alone — a meaningful business, but one that lacked the end-to-end story hyperscaler procurement teams increasingly demanded from strategic infrastructure suppliers. With Infinera integrated, Nokia could position the combined IP Networks plus Optical Networks capability as a unified fabric for AI campus buildout. The strategic logic was coherent. The execution would be measured quarter by quarter across the Hotard era that had, by the frozen window of May 23, 2026, only just begun.

chapters.title: Justin Hotard, Marco Wirén CFO, segment leadership, and the Baldauf-chaired board
chapters.body:
## The Succession

On 10 February 2025, Nokia filed a brief inside-information announcement on the Helsinki Stock Exchange that ended five years of continuity at the top of Europe's largest telecommunications equipment maker. Pekka Lundmark, who had returned to Nokia in August 2020 calling it "a homecoming" and spent the intervening years dismantling a ruinously broad product portfolio, would step down. His successor was an American engineer who had spent the preceding year leading Intel Corporation's Data Center & AI Group: Justin Hotard, aged 51, effective 1 April 2025. The transition was swift. Lundmark agreed to remain as an advisor to the incoming chief executive through the end of 2025, providing continuity across the February close of the Infinera acquisition and the first earnings cycle under the new leadership.

Sari Baldauf, Nokia's board chair since 2020, framed the appointment in the strategic terms that mattered most to investors watching the company's AI data-centre pivot:

> "I am delighted to welcome Justin to Nokia. He has a strong track record of accelerating growth in technology companies along with vast expertise in AI and data center markets, which are critical areas for Nokia's future growth."

Hotard, for his part, used the announcement to invoke the infrastructure-as-backbone thesis that would animate his early tenure:

> "Networks are the backbone that power society and businesses, and enable generational technology shifts like the one we are currently experiencing in AI. I am excited to get started and look forward to continuing Nokia's transformation journey to maximize its potential for growth and value creation."

[Nokia 6-K, SEC EDGAR, filed 10 February 2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/924613/000110465925011052/)

---

## Justin Hotard: Formation and Mandate

Hotard's formation is that of a systems-and-scale engineer who moved steadily toward general management. He took a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in 1997 and joined Motorola as a systems engineer before completing an MBA at MIT's Sloan School of Management in 2002. The subsequent career traced the arc of enterprise technology infrastructure: corporate development and product management at Symbol Technologies (acquired by Motorola), then a seven-year stint at NCR Corporation building cloud and small-business platform businesses, before a decade-long ascent at Hewlett Packard Enterprise. At HPE he ran country operations in Japan and China, then became executive vice president and general manager of the High Performance Computing, AI & Labs division — precisely the moment, 2015 to 2024, when HPC clusters began absorbing the deep-learning workloads that would reshape the entire networking market. Intel recruited him in 2024 to lead its Data Center & AI Group, the division responsible for Xeon and Gaudi, just as Nokia's board was assembling a succession list weighted toward AI-infrastructure expertise.

That résumé produced exactly the operating profile Nokia's board sought. The company's IP Networks routing portfolio — inherited from Alcatel-Lucent in the January 2016 acquisition — had identified the hyperscaler data centre as its principal adjacent market, and Lundmark's final earnings statement, delivered in January 2025, committed up to €100 million in additional annual operating expenditure to drive €1 billion of incremental data-centre networking revenue by 2028. Hotard arrived as the investment mandate was being funded and the sales motion was beginning.

---

## First Weeks in Charge

The Q1 2025 interim report, filed 24 April 2025, contained Hotard's first formal statement to shareholders — delivered after only three weeks in the role. It was at once diagnostic, reassuring, and cautious about the rapidly shifting tariff environment:

> "Since joining Nokia as President and CEO three weeks ago, I've had great engagements with some of our customers, partners and employees. I see great potential for Nokia, and my early focus is on capital allocation to ensure we both drive efficiency and invest sufficiently in the right growth segments for long-term value creation. I am impressed with our core technology base across our portfolio including in RAN and core as well as in IP, Optical and Fiber technologies. In speaking with customers, it is clear we play a critical role as a trusted partner operating their mobile and fixed networks and have the potential to expand our presence in hyperscale, enterprise and defense markets."

[Nokia Q1 2025 Interim Report, SEC EDGAR 6-K, filed 24 April 2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/924613/000110465925038218/)

The underlying numbers were mixed. Group net sales fell 3% on a constant-currency, comparable-portfolio basis to €4,390 million, but stripped of the prior-year Nokia Technologies catch-up, organic growth was 7%. Network Infrastructure — the business group most directly tied to Hotard's mandate — advanced 11% in constant currency, with Optical Networks expanding 15% in its first full quarter incorporating Infinera capacity. Mobile Networks grew 2% but absorbed an unexpected €120 million contract-settlement charge from a single customer project dating to 2019, compressing comparable operating margin sharply. Hotard left the full-year comparable operating profit guidance of €1.9 billion to €2.4 billion unchanged while warning that tariff disruption could subtract €20–30 million from Q2 comparable operating profit. A capital markets day, intended to deliver the complete value-creation framework, was scheduled for November 2025.

---

## Marco Wirén: The Financial Architecture

Chief Financial Officer Marco Wirén, who joined Nokia in 2020, brings a distinctively Nordic industrials pedigree to the role. Born in 1966 and holding a master's degree in business administration from Uppsala University, Wirén spent the first decade of his career in corporate development and strategic planning at NCC Group before moving to Eltel Networks — a Scandinavian power-line and telecoms-infrastructure services group — where he served successively as head of service division, VP of business development, and CFO. He joined SSAB, the Swedish-Finnish steelmaker, as CFO in 2008 and held the role for five years, before moving to Wärtsilä Corporation, the Finnish marine and energy technology company, first as group CFO and then as president of the energy division. The Wärtsilä energy presidency — running a capital-intensive equipment business selling to utilities and power generators — provided the operating-side exposure that distinguishes Wirén from a pure finance profile.

At Nokia, Wirén also carries formal designation as Chief Risk Officer, overseeing the enterprise risk management framework across the group. His tenure has spanned the decisive restructuring years: the shedding of the submarine networks infrastructure centre under Lundmark, the multi-year decline and partial recovery in mobile networks demand, the Infinera acquisition financing, and the transition to Hotard's AI data-centre strategic posture. He held a board seat at Neste Corporation from 2015 to 2023, adding listed-company governance depth alongside the operational CFO role.

---

## Segment Leadership

The group leadership team that Hotard inherited is built around four business group presidents with markedly different institutional histories.

**Federico Guillén**, President of Network Infrastructure since early 2023, is the executive most directly accountable for translating the AI data-centre thesis into revenue. A telecommunications engineer by training — degree from the Escuela Técnica Superior de Ingenieros de Telecomunicación at Universidad Politécnica de Madrid — Guillén joined the Nokia group leadership team in 2016 following the Alcatel-Lucent acquisition, where he had served as president of fixed networks. His Network Infrastructure remit covers IP Networks (the SR Linux routing platform now marketed to hyperscalers), Optical Networks (substantially enlarged by Infinera), Fixed Networks (fibre access), and Submarine Networks. It is the business group Lundmark singled out in his January 2025 farewell remarks for its 17% net sales acceleration in Q4 2024, with IP Networks alone growing 24% year-on-year as North American carrier investment recovered.

**Tommi Uitto**, President of Mobile Networks, is Nokia's longest-tenured business group president, having joined the company in 1996 and accumulated three decades of radio-access-network operating experience across Nokia's various corporate iterations — Nokia Networks, Nokia Siemens Networks, and the post-Alcatel-Lucent group. His division reported net sales of €1,729 million in Q1 2025, roughly flat year-on-year in underlying terms, as the post-5G-investment-cycle stabilisation that Lundmark began describing in late 2023 continued. Uitto secured a notable contract extension with T-Mobile US during the quarter.

**Raghav Sahgal**, President of Cloud and Network Services, joined Nokia in 2017 from the enterprise software world and has led the business group since 2020. CNS delivered 8% net sales growth in Q1 2025, driven by 5G core wins at AT&T, Boost Mobile, Ooredoo Qatar, and Telefónica. **Patrik Hammarén**, an eighteen-year Nokia lawyer who holds a master of law from the University of Helsinki, became acting president of Nokia Technologies in January 2025 following the departure of Jenni Lukander; the patent licensing business, which monetises Nokia's multi-decade intellectual property portfolio, entered 2025 with a contracted annual net sales run-rate of approximately €1.4 billion. Two newer additions to the broader leadership team add non-traditional depth: **Nishant Batra**, Chief Strategy and Technology Officer (joined 2021, ex-Ericsson and Veoneer), leads forward technology positioning; **Mikko Hautala**, Chief Geopolitical and Government Relations Officer (joined 2024), brings a decade's experience as a Finnish career diplomat — including postings as ambassador in Moscow and Washington — to a company whose network infrastructure is embedded in the critical infrastructure of dozens of states and whose competitive environment is shaped as much by export-control policy as by technology.

---

## The Baldauf-Chaired Board

Sari Baldauf, 70, has chaired Nokia's board since 2020, having joined as a non-executive director in 2018. Her Nokia career in an earlier era — executive vice president and general manager of the Networks Business Group from 1998 to 2005 — spanned the peak of Nokia's mobile-equipment dominance and the early consolidation of what would become the IP Networks and optical inheritance of the Alcatel-Lucent acquisition. She subsequently served as chair of Fortum Corporation and on the supervisory boards of both Deutsche Telekom and Mercedes-Benz Group before returning to Nokia governance. It is a profile calibrated for exactly the kind of oversight the company has required across three CEO transitions in a decade.

The board that Baldauf chairs underwent meaningful renewal at the annual general meeting of 29 April 2025. Two departures — Søren Skou, the former Maersk chief executive who had served as vice chair, and Carla Smits-Nusteling — were replaced by two appointments that reinforced the AI data-centre and telecom-operator strategic logic. **Timo Ihamuotila**, currently CFO of ABB and Nokia's own group CFO from 2009 to 2016, was elected as the new vice chair, re-introducing deep institutional knowledge of Nokia's financial structure at a moment of significant capital-allocation decisions. **Pernille Erenbjerg**, former chief executive of Denmark's TDC Group, brought direct telecom-operator CEO experience to a board that already included **Lisa Hook**, the former Neustar president and chief executive, as its principal carrier-side voice.

The five standing committees reflect the complexity of a multi-business-group company navigating simultaneous technology transitions. **Thomas Dannenfeldt** — CFO of Deutsche Telekom from 2014 to 2018 — chairs both the Audit Committee and the Personnel Committee, providing financial rigour informed by direct knowledge of Nokia's largest European customer category. **Kai Öistämö**, who served as Nokia's chief development officer through the devices era and now runs Vaisala Corporation, chairs the Technology Committee, joined by **Thomas Saueressig** of SAP's executive board and **Mike McNamara**, the former Target CIO. **Elizabeth Crain**, co-founder of Moelis & Company and a veteran of UBS investment banking, chairs the Strategy Committee — the committee most directly engaged with the AI data-centre pivot and the capital markets day that Hotard had pencilled in for November 2025.

The resulting governance structure pairs a chair with thirty years of Nokia institutional memory against a chief executive whose entire operational formation occurred in the data-centre infrastructure markets Nokia was now entering. Whether that combination could convert a legacy carrier-equipment franchise into a credible hyperscaler routing partner was the central question Hotard was expected to answer, in measurable revenue terms, by the time the frozen window closed in May 2026.

chapters.title: Telecom carriers, hyperscaler AI data centres, patent licensees
chapters.body:
Nokia's commercial reach in 2025 divided along three distinct customer vectors: the telecom carriers that had anchored the company's core equipment franchise for decades; the hyperscale data centre operators who emerged as the defining growth opportunity under new chief executive Justin Hotard; and the technology patent licensees that delivered some of the company's highest-margin recurring revenue through Nokia Technologies. Binding these customer relationships together was a supply chain that spanned proprietary photonic integrated circuits in the optical layer, merchant network silicon in the routing layer, and a geographically dispersed contract manufacturing base navigating its own geopolitical pressures.

## The Carrier Franchise

Nokia's telecom carrier customer base represented the company's deepest and most durable revenue foundation. By early 2025, Nokia maintained active supply relationships with operators across well over sixty countries, covering every generation of wireless standards from LTE-Advanced through 5G New Radio. In North America, AT&T, Verizon Communications, and T-Mobile US anchored the Mobile Networks revenue base; Nokia had defended substantial 5G RAN share against Nordic rival Ericsson and Korean challenger Samsung Networks. Across Europe, the roster read like a directory of the continent's incumbent operators: Deutsche Telekom, Vodafone Group, Orange, BT Group, and Telefónica among them. In Asia, SoftBank and NTT DoCoMo in Japan, SK Telecom in South Korea, and Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel in India represented major engagements. Nokia had supplied the Jio 5G rollout—one of the world's most ambitious greenfield deployments—from its outset, cementing a strategic foothold in what became the world's largest 5G subscriber market by volume.

Nokia's share of the global 5G RAN addressable market held in the high-single-digit percentage range, with Ericsson and Nokia together representing the principal Western-aligned supply alternative to Huawei — a structural tailwind that partially offset the cyclical pressure of the 2022-2024 carrier spending correction.

The Network Infrastructure segment's Fixed Networks and Submarine Networks units rounded out the carrier customer roster. Fixed Networks—fibre-to-the-premises and fibre-to-the-home access equipment—counted major European and North American broadband operators among its customers, including AT&T's fibre expansion programme and European incumbents accelerating FTTH rollouts as regulatory fibre mandates tightened. Submarine Networks served a more specialised clientele: the consortia and private undersea cable operators laying transoceanic capacity, including routes partially backed by the same hyperscalers who were simultaneously emerging as Nokia's most strategically consequential new customer class.

## Hyperscaler Engagement: Optical Networks and the AI Router Opportunity

The February 2025 Infinera close transformed Nokia's Optical Networks segment and imported a hyperscaler customer base. Infinera's engagements included [Microsoft](https://www.nokia.com/investors/) and a broader set of North American hyperscaler accounts — giving the combined entity a foothold within the purchasing organisations of the world's largest cloud operators.

SR Linux — the cloud-native routing OS built on the Alcatel-Lucent heritage — combined with Infinera's optical layer gave Nokia a structural differentiator: the only vendor able to offer both IP routing and coherent optical transport under a single engineering roadmap. Hotard framed this vertical integration as critical at a moment when AI cluster architectures demanded tighter coordination between optical transport and the routing fabric above it.

The competitive table as Nokia's management assessed it entering 2025 looked approximately as follows:

| Vendor | Optical Layer | IP Routing Layer | AI Data Centre Positioning |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nokia (post-Infinera) | Nokia Optical / Infinera PICs | SR Linux, 7750 SR | Optical + routing integration |
| Cisco Systems | Cisco Optical (ORi heritage) | IOS XR, Silicon One ASIC | Full-stack, proprietary silicon |
| Arista Networks | Limited | EOS, 7800R | Ethernet switching/routing focus |
| Ciena | WaveLogic coherent | Limited | Optical specialist |
| Infinera (pre-Nokia) | ICE6 / GX PICs | Limited | Optical specialist |

## Patent Licensees: Nokia Technologies

Nokia Technologies — the licensing operation built on standards-essential patents covering 2G through 5G NR — generated revenue of approximately €1.1–1.4 billion annually at margins substantially above Nokia's consolidated average. The licensee roster encompassed Apple, Samsung, Xiaomi, Oppo, Vivo, and the broader Android OEM ecosystem, alongside an expanding automotive telematics and enterprise IoT customer base.

## Supply Chain: Photonic Integration, Merchant Silicon, and Contract Manufacturing

Nokia's supply chain bore the imprint of its acquisition history and the divergent technical architectures of its two principal networking layers.

In Optical Networks, the Infinera acquisition imported a genuinely proprietary supply position. Infinera had developed and manufactured its own Photonic Integrated Circuits based on Indium Phosphide semiconductor technology, co-integrating transmitter, modulator, amplifier, and receiver functions onto a single die rather than assembling them from discrete components sourced externally. This in-house PIC fabrication—conducted at Infinera's own wafer-level facility—provided supply chain insulation against the component shortages that had afflicted optical vendors dependent on third-party PIC foundries, and conferred a technology differentiation that commodity-sourcing competitors could not easily replicate. The InP substrate supply chain introduced its own upstream concentration: Indium Phosphide wafers were sourced from a small number of global producers, and wafer supply remained a potential bottleneck in scenarios of rapid demand acceleration or geopolitical disruption to key producing nations.

In IP Networks routing, Nokia had made a deliberately contrasting architectural choice: SR Linux ran on hardware built around merchant silicon, principally from suppliers including Broadcom and Marvell Technology. That decision—distinguishing Nokia from Cisco's vertically integrated custom-ASIC approach—reflected the strategic judgement that differentiation resided in the operating system, protocol stack, and programmability model rather than in proprietary forwarding silicon. Merchant silicon exposure aligned Nokia's routing economics with the disaggregated networking market's cost trajectory, while concentrating R&D investment where Nokia believed the defensible advantage resided.

Final assembly and systems integration for Nokia's hardware portfolio proceeded through a combination of Nokia-operated facilities—including the long-established Oulu, Finland manufacturing site—and external contract manufacturers. Nokia had accelerated efforts to diversify its electronics manufacturing geography in response to the geopolitical reshaping of global supply chains, pursuing production options in India as that government incentivised domestic electronics assembly through its Production Linked Incentive scheme. The Nokia India presence, spanning both supply chain operations and a substantial software engineering workforce, positioned the company to serve Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel's continued network expansion from in-country operations while satisfying those operators' emerging preferences for locally assembled network equipment—a regulatory and procurement alignment that competitors without an established Indian manufacturing footprint would need years to replicate.

chapters.title: Where Nokia sits against Ericsson, Cisco, Juniper, Arista, Huawei, broader
chapters.body:
## The Shape of the Battlefield

Nokia's competitive map divides along two axes: the telco access layer, where it confronts Ericsson and Huawei; and the networking layer — routers, switches, optical transport — where Cisco, Juniper, and Arista set the terms. The Infinera acquisition and Hotard succession declared the second axis primary.

## The Ericsson Duel: Parity with Diverging Trajectories

In fifth-generation radio access, Nokia and Ericsson have fought to a rough draw across the Western carrier market for the better part of a decade. Both benefited materially from regulatory bans on Huawei equipment across the United States, United Kingdom, Sweden, and Australia, forcing rip-and-replace programmes that handed Nokia and Ericsson the bulk of North American and Western European buildouts from 2020 onward.

The similarity ends there. Ericsson's strategic ambitions remain anchored to mobile — Ericsson Packet Core, Ericsson Radio System, managed services — with relatively limited exposure to the IP routing and optical transport layers now in Nokia's favour. Nokia's Network Infrastructure segment, which houses IP Networks, Optical Networks, Fixed Networks, and Submarine Networks, had no direct Ericsson equivalent. When Hotard took the stage at Nokia's first-quarter 2025 earnings presentation, he drew that distinction explicitly: Nokia's ability to pursue what he described as the "convergence of IP and optical" was, in his framing, a differentiation that pure-play radio vendors could not replicate.

Ericsson has meanwhile absorbed the reputational and financial consequences of the United States Department of Justice proceedings tied to corruption in Iraq — a matter that constrained its American expansion and thinned executive bandwidth through the mid-2020s. Nokia has not been free of governance strain — its own profit warnings in 2023 triggered a significant share sell-off — but it entered the Hotard era without the legal cloud that shadowed Stockholm. On the 5G front, Dell'Oro Group data placed Nokia and Ericsson within a few percentage points of each other in Western RAN market share through 2024, with Samsung closing ground in North America and South Korea.

## Cisco: The Routing Incumbent

In service-provider IP routing, Cisco's dominance is structural. Its IOS XR operating system runs on the ASR 9000 and NCS platforms that anchor backbone and peering infrastructure across most of the world's largest telcos. Nokia inherited, via the January 2016 Alcatel-Lucent acquisition, a credible challenger in the 7750 Service Router family and its SR OS platform. That heritage gave Nokia a foothold in carrier core routing that no other European vendor possesses.

The competitive tension has sharpened as data centre fabric and carrier core routing converge. Nokia's SR Linux — an open, container-native network operating system built from scratch — sits at the centre of its hyperscaler and AI data centre pitch. Where Cisco's NX-OS and its Nexus switching portfolio dominate legacy enterprise and carrier data centre fabric, Nokia's proposition is that SR Linux's programmability and its native integration with telemetry and automation toolchains make it better suited for AI training cluster networking, where east-west traffic volumes dwarf anything classical spine-leaf designs were engineered for.

Cisco's scale advantage — revenues in the high-USD 50 billion range through fiscal 2025, against Nokia's €22-23 billion envelope — is formidable. But Cisco's routing revenue has faced pressure from the same AI-driven shift that Hotard is exploiting: hyperscalers building custom silicon and white-box switching are eroding Cisco's data centre margin profile, creating space for software-forward challengers willing to run on merchant silicon.

## Juniper and the HPE Variable

Juniper Networks — the service-provider router vendor that the MX Series placed as Nokia's closest direct competitor in carrier IP/MPLS — is now mid-absorption into Hewlett Packard Enterprise. The deal, announced in January 2023 and cleared by the European Commission and US Department of Justice after extended review, closed in 2024. The integration has occupied Juniper's commercial and engineering leadership through most of the period when Nokia was integrating Infinera and repositioning toward AI data centres.

For Nokia, the Juniper-HPE combination is a double-edged development. On one hand, an absorbed Juniper may accelerate in enterprise distribution, a channel Nokia has historically underserved; HPE's Aruba networking business could pull Juniper intelligence toward campus and branch, dimming its carrier focus. On the other hand, HPE's balance sheet and procurement relationships with hyperscalers could accelerate Juniper's own data centre ambitions. The outcome remains unresolved within the frozen window.

| Vendor | Primary Segment | 2024 Revenue (approx.) | IP/Optical Exposure |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nokia | Telco + AI DC (emerging) | €22–23bn | Full stack: IP routing, optical, fixed, submarine |
| Ericsson | Telco RAN + managed services | SEK ~250–260bn (~€22bn) | Minimal routing/optical |
| Cisco | Enterprise + carrier networking | USD ~57bn | Dominant in routing; optical via Acacia |
| Juniper/HPE | Carrier + enterprise routing | USD ~5–6bn (standalone) | Service-provider routing, growing DC |
| Arista | Cloud/AI data centre | USD ~7–8bn | DC switching dominant; limited carrier |
| Huawei | Full telco stack | CNY ~700bn (~€88bn) | Full stack; restricted in West |

## Arista: The Data Centre Incumbent Nokia Must Displace

If Ericsson is Nokia's equal-weight adversary in radio, Arista Networks is the dominant force Nokia must challenge if the AI data centre routing thesis is to pay out. Arista's EOS — the single-image operating system that runs across its entire switch and router portfolio — has made it the default fabric vendor for hyperscalers, cloud-native enterprises, and, since 2022, for the GPU cluster networks that underpin AI training at scale. Microsoft, Meta, and major cloud providers are Arista reference customers.

Nokia's SR Linux competes on programmability, disaggregation, and openness. Its partnership with Microsoft — reported in industry coverage through 2024 and 2025 as Nokia engaged Azure infrastructure teams on IP fabric deployments — was the clearest early signal that the SR Linux platform was earning hyperscaler credence. But Arista's installed base, its deep EOS automation ecosystem, and its gross margin profile (historically above 60 percent) reflect a product-market fit that Nokia has not yet matched at scale in the data centre layer.

Hotard's competitive edge here is architectural: Nokia can offer a coherent IP-over-optical stack — 7750 SR routers feeding directly into Nokia's WDM optical transport, now dramatically expanded by Infinera's ICE6 and ICE-X coherent optics platforms — that Arista cannot replicate. Arista sells Ethernet switching. Nokia, post-Infinera, can sell the switching layer and the photonic layer in a single commercial relationship, which matters to hyperscalers seeking to compress the number of infrastructure vendors operating inside their campuses and long-haul corridors.

## Huawei: The Constrained Giant

Huawei's telecom equipment division remains formidable in Asia, the Middle East, Africa, and Latin America. In the West, regulatory restrictions since 2019 — UK Telecoms Security Act, US NDAA Section 889, and equivalent legislation — have transferred legacy Huawei positions to Nokia and Ericsson through rip-and-replace contracts, while insulating Nokia's data centre pitch from Huawei's CloudEngine portfolio.

## Nokia Technologies: The Licensing Moat

None of Nokia's named competitors can match the Nokia Technologies patent licensing income — a high-margin buffer that scales with global device shipments rather than carrier capex cycles. Ericsson has a comparable but smaller licensing unit; Cisco, Juniper, and Arista have no equivalent.

## The Integrated Stack as Differentiator

The argument Hotard inherited, and which he has sharpened toward AI data centre audiences, is that Nokia's breadth is itself a competitive weapon. An Arista-only data centre vendor must source optical transport from Ciena or Coherent. A Cisco-dominant carrier must layer in third-party optical. Nokia's post-Infinera stack — SR Linux fabric, 7750 SR routers, PSE-4 and PSE-V custom photonic silicon, Infinera ICE-X coherent modules, and Nokia Wavelength Routing Mesh — offers a single-vendor coherent IP-optical architecture from server rack to intercontinental submarine cable.

> "We have a unique combination of IP and optical that others simply can't replicate," Hotard said at the Nokia Capital Markets Day in late 2025, framing the integrated portfolio as the primary basis for differentiation in AI data centre fabric bids.

Whether the integration discount that markets have historically applied to diversified telecom vendors converts to an integration premium in an AI infrastructure cycle — where hyperscalers place enormous value on operational simplicity and single-vendor accountability — is the central competitive bet of the Hotard era. The field against which that bet plays out, from Ericsson's radio dominance to Arista's data centre hegemony to Cisco's routing incumbency, is formidable. Nokia's edges — optical scale from Infinera, Alcatel-Lucent's IP routing pedigree, the patent licensing cushion, and the Western market shelter from Huawei — are real. Whether they compound into durable market share gains remains the open question of 2026 and beyond.

chapters.title: From 2016 Alcatel-Lucent through Lundmark, Infinera, Hotard
chapters.body:
## The Alcatel-Lucent Inheritance

The January 2016 Alcatel-Lucent acquisition — detailed in the Corporate History chapter — brought the IP Networks routing portfolio and Bell Labs optical transmission heritage that would, a decade later, become the architecture for Nokia's AI data centre positioning. [Nokia press release, April 2015](https://www.nokia.com/investors/)

## The Lundmark Restructuring, 2020–2025

Pekka Lundmark arrived at Nokia's Espoo headquarters in August 2020 as successor to Suri, who had led the company since 2014. Lundmark, previously chief executive of Fortum, the Finnish energy utility, inherited a company that had stumbled in the early 5G deployment wave — losing share to Ericsson and facing margin compression — and a revenue base that would peak approaching €25 billion during the post-COVID 5G spending surge before beginning a sustained contraction.

Lundmark's central strategic move was a declared R&D investment acceleration, directing capital back into the 5G radio and network silicon programmes that had fallen behind under Suri's later tenure. The restructuring, which included reductions of roughly ten thousand employees over 2020–2022, was framed as freeing capital for technology reinvestment rather than straightforward cost reduction. The multi-year operational framework Lundmark established — with CFO Marco Wirén, who joined from Wärtsilä in January 2021 — set the financial architecture against which the Infinera deal and the Hotard succession were subsequently layered.

By late 2024, as carrier capital expenditure cycles moderated globally and the 5G peak subsided, Nokia's annual revenue had compressed to approximately €19.7 billion (~$21 billion) — down roughly 21 per cent from the 2022 peak. The structural challenge was visible: Mobile Networks, historically the largest segment, faced pricing pressure and a customer mix increasingly weighted toward cost-sensitive tier-two operators as Tier 1 US carriers completed their initial 5G rollouts.

The Network Infrastructure segment — the Alcatel-Lucent-heritage franchise spanning IP Networks routing, Optical Networks, Fixed Networks, and Submarine Networks, led by Federico Guillen since January 2023 — was by late 2024 the business group in which Nokia's next strategic chapter would have to be written.

## The Infinera Transaction

In June 2024, Nokia announced it had agreed to acquire Infinera Corporation, the Santa Clara-based optical networking equipment vendor, for approximately $2.3 billion in a combined cash and all-stock transaction. [Nokia announcement, June 2024](https://www.nokia.com/investors/) The deal represented the most significant optical networking M&A move since Nokia-Alcatel-Lucent itself.

Infinera brought a design-led optical systems capability based in California, a Latin American carrier customer base that complemented Nokia's existing European and Asian footprint, and — critically — hyperscaler optical transport customer relationships that Nokia's internal optical business had not established at comparable depth. The PSM-series coherent optical systems and the Infinera engineering organisation represented genuine additions to the Nokia portfolio rather than a consolidation play.

The transaction closed February 28, 2025 — thirty-three days before Justin Hotard formally assumed the CEO role. The timing was not incidental: the Infinera integration was structured as a foundational piece of the incoming CEO's strategic platform rather than a legacy transaction to be managed around. The combined Optical Networks entity substantially scaled Nokia's presence in the hyperscaler optical infrastructure market — precisely the customer segment Hotard would subsequently address with the IP Networks routing portfolio.

## The Hotard Succession

Justin Hotard's appointment as CEO effective April 1, 2025 represented a deliberate break from the Scandinavian-industrial succession pattern. The board reached into the hyperscaler supply chain executive cohort — Hotard's Intel and HPE data-centre background — rather than the telecom equipment industry, signalling that the IP Networks routing portfolio was Nokia's forward growth thesis.

## Forward Catalysts

The strategic agenda under Hotard as of the frozen snapshot date converged on three operational milestones that would define Nokia's competitive trajectory through 2026.

The first was the Infinera integration timeline. The February 2025 close initiated a multi-quarter process of customer base rationalisation, supply chain consolidation, and product portfolio integration across Nokia's legacy Optical Networks business and Infinera's PSM-series coherent optical systems. The hyperscaler optical transport relationships acquired through Infinera were the primary near-term revenue expansion opportunity — and the pace of integration execution would determine whether those relationships deepened or eroded to competitors.

The second was the AI data centre router commercial programme. Nokia's SR Linux platform on FP5 silicon entered the AI data centre routing market as a challenger to Arista's EOS-on-Ethernet installed base and Cisco's Nexus franchise. The Microsoft engagement — representing a reference-quality hyperscaler validation — was the central commercial milestone. Quarterly order progression in the data centre router category under Guillen's Network Infrastructure group was, by early 2026, the most closely watched near-term financial signal at Nokia.

The third was Hotard's capital allocation posture toward Network Infrastructure relative to Mobile Networks. The revenue compression in the carrier-facing Mobile Networks segment provided both the financial pressure and the strategic rationale for accelerating the AI data centre pivot. How Hotard calibrated R&D spend between the two largest business groups — and whether Network Infrastructure's margin profile could absorb the investment required to win hyperscaler router contracts at scale against incumbents with decades of installed base — was the defining medium-term strategic question.

Nokia's competitive position through 2026 would be substantially determined by whether the Alcatel-Lucent routing heritage, the Infinera optical acquisition, and the Hotard AI-data-centre strategic mandate cohered into a commercial programme capable of generating durable revenue growth.
