The Lundmark era had stabilised the operational and financial foundation. The Infinera transaction had scaled the optical footprint. The question Hotard's tenure would answer was whether a Finnish telecommunications equipment vendor, through a chain of acquisitions from Bell Labs to Infinera, had assembled the pieces to take a meaningful share of the infrastructure spend underpinning the AI buildout.

chapters.title: 5G IP, IP Networks SR Linux, Optical Networks technology, Bell Labs
chapters.body:
## The Alcatel-Lucent Inheritance

Nokia's technology depth in IP routing and optical transport is overwhelmingly an Alcatel-Lucent inheritance — augmented by the February 2025 Infinera close and reoriented under Hotard's data-centre mandate.

## SR Linux and the Data Centre Router Opportunity

The most consequential platform Nokia produced in the Lundmark era is SR Linux, a cloud-native network operating system launched in 2020 as a deliberate break from the proprietary software model the company had maintained since the 7750 Service Router family first shipped in the mid-2000s. SR Linux runs as containerised microservices, exposes a fully programmable, model-driven interface via gNMI and gRPC, and was designed from the ground up for hyperscaler workflows — specifically for engineering teams that deploy infrastructure through GitOps pipelines rather than CLI sessions.

The platform runs on Nokia's 7250 IXR (Interconnect Router) family, powered by Nokia's fifth-generation FP5 forwarding processor. FP5 — designed in-house at Nokia's Ottawa silicon team — delivers line-rate programmable forwarding with integrated telemetry and was specifically architected to handle the east-west traffic patterns of AI training clusters, where hundreds of GPU servers exchange gradient updates in tightly scheduled all-reduce collectives. That distinction matters: traditional service-provider routers optimise for north-south subscriber flows; the AI data centre requires routers that can sustain terabit-scale, low-latency mesh topologies with deterministic jitter and congestion-aware load balancing.

The hyperscaler validation Nokia secured through 2023 and 2024 included Microsoft Azure, which deployed Nokia's IP routing fabric within Azure data-centre interconnect infrastructure, as reported by [Light Reading](https://www.lightreading.com). Nokia distinguished itself from incumbent data-centre switch vendors by offering a fully open NOS that operators could extend through standard YANG models and Python-based event-handler scripts — a posture that resonated with hyperscaler teams accustomed to running their own network automation stacks.

On Nokia's Q4 2024 earnings call, Pekka Lundmark framed the strategic logic:

> "AI is driving a fundamental rethinking of what network infrastructure needs to do. IP Networks is extremely well positioned. We have the products, we have the customers, and we are winning."

When Justin Hotard assumed the CEO chair on April 1, 2025, he sharpened the message. Arriving from Intel's Data Center and AI Group, where he had led product strategy sold directly into the same hyperscaler accounts Nokia was courting, Hotard signalled that SR Linux would be treated not as a niche routing win but as a platform business requiring a dedicated go-to-market motion:

> "Nokia has the routing technology that the AI data centre needs. My job is to make sure we're having the right conversations at the right level inside these customers — and that we're building the services and software layer that makes Nokia a strategic partner, not just a vendor."

## 5G Transport: The Mobile Backhaul and Fronthaul Stack

SR Linux's data-centre trajectory does not displace Nokia's foundational role as the IP transport layer for 5G mobile networks. The company's 7705 SAR (Service Aggregation Router) and 7750 SR families carry the backhaul and midhaul traffic connecting 5G radio units, distributed units, and centralised units across the F1, F2, and NG interfaces that define Open RAN and disaggregated 5G architectures.

Nokia's Mobile Networks business group contributed roughly 40% of group net sales through the mid-2020s, and the routing equipment that IP Networks supplies to 5G operators created a durable bundling dynamic: carriers deploying Nokia's AirScale ReefShark SoC radios tended to purchase the Nokia IP transport stack for its timing-synchronisation compatibility (IEEE 1588v2 / SyncE) and native segment-routing support (SR-MPLS and SRv6). That cross-business dependency supported IP Networks' margin through the initial 5G rollout cycle but also exposed Nokia to mobile capex fluctuations.

By 2025, with North American and European Tier 1 operators having largely completed initial 5G NR macro deployments, the incremental growth narrative within IP Networks had shifted decisively toward the data centre — precisely the rotation Hotard's mandate was constructed to capture.

## Optical Networks: The Infinera Augmentation

Before Infinera, Nokia's optical portfolio traced to Alcatel's 1830 PSS platform and coherent DSP silicon (PSE-3, PSE-3s, PSE-V) from Nokia's Lannion engineering team. Infinera added three capabilities: the ICE6 coherent DSP for 800G spectral efficiency (positioning Nokia for 1.6T via ICE7), the GX Series open line systems with strong NA Tier 1 penetration, and submarine cable management software inherited from Coriant.

| Optical asset | Origin | Core capability |
|---|---|---|
| 1830 PSS platform | Alcatel heritage | Metro and long-haul DWDM switching |
| PSE-V coherent DSP | Nokia Lannion | 1.2 Tb/s per wavelength |
| ICE6 coherent DSP | Infinera San Jose | 800G, open pluggable |
| GX Series open line | Infinera | NA Tier 1 and cable penetration |
| Submarine NMS | Coriant / Infinera | End-to-end submarine cable management |

The combined optical portfolio placed Nokia in direct competition with Ciena Corporation across all three major optical segments: long-haul DWDM, metro coherent, and submarine.

## Nokia Bell Labs

Bell Labs remains the most symbolically significant asset Nokia holds. Founded as Bell Telephone Laboratories in 1925 and the birthplace of the transistor (1947), information theory (Claude Shannon, 1948), Unix, and the C programming language, the institution arrived at Nokia through Alcatel-Lucent and has been maintained at its Murray Hill, New Jersey campus as an active research organisation.

Under Nokia's stewardship, Bell Labs concentrated its long-horizon work on three clusters: future network architectures, including 6G air-interface research contributing to the 3GPP Release 20 standardisation cycle; applied AI for network operations, autonomous network management, and energy minimisation; and quantum networking, specifically quantum key distribution (QKD) for carrier-grade cryptographic applications. The institution publishes in *Nature*, *Science*, and top-tier IEEE venues, and holds thousands of active patents — a stock that complements rather than duplicates the broader Nokia licensing portfolio.

The institutional credibility of Bell Labs functions as a recruitment and partnership instrument that Nokia's principal competitors — Ericsson, which dismantled its own research lab infrastructure through successive restructurings; and Cisco, which absorbed Bell Labs-era talent but never held the brand — cannot readily replicate.

## Patent Portfolio and Nokia Technologies

Nokia is one of the five largest declared holders of 5G SEPs globally. Beyond licensing economics (€1.3–1.5 billion annually at high margins), Nokia's standing in 3GPP and IEEE standardisation bodies gives its engineering teams direct influence over whether SR Linux's SRv6 extensions, Bell Labs' 6G proposals, or Infinera's coherent optics specifications become industry baseline — upstream leverage that pure-hardware competitors cannot access.

chapters.title: Telecom cycle, Ericsson competition, AI cycle, Huawei dynamics, patent licensing
chapters.body:
## A Cycle That Gave and Then Took Away

The 21 percent revenue decline from 2022 peak to 2024 — detailed in the Financial chapter — exposed Nokia's structural exposure to carrier capex cycles. [Nokia Investor Relations](https://www.nokia.com/investors/) The risk is that the next telecom capex cycle could be both smaller and more distributed in vendor share than the 5G wave it follows.

## The Nordic Rival and the Korean Disruptor

Within that compressed carrier market, Nokia faced intensifying competition from its closest peer. Ericsson, also headquartered in the Nordic region and also rebuilt on a decade of restructuring, had stabilised its own finances and regained commercial aggression in the Radio Access Network market. [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/) The two companies had effectively divided the global 5G vendor landscape among themselves and Samsung Networks wherever Huawei and ZTE were restricted — but that oligopoly structure provided only partial protection.

Samsung Networks was the more disruptive competitive threat in the medium term. The South Korean conglomerate had demonstrated in the United States — most visibly through its Dish Network and T-Mobile contracts — that its integrated semiconductor-to-software-to-antenna architecture could deliver competitive performance at aggressive price points. As more operators began re-architecting networks with Open RAN-compliant interfaces, Samsung's willingness to subsidise market entry with hardware margin compression posed a direct challenge to Nokia's installed base in key accounts.

The financial stakes were significant. Mobile Networks accounted for a substantial share of Nokia's overall revenue, and the segment's margins were already under pressure from the volume declines of 2023 and 2024. Any further share loss to Ericsson in Europe or Samsung in Asia-Pacific and North America would compound the cycle headwind with a structural one.

## The Hyperscaler Bet and Its Inherent Uncertainty

The AI data centre routing opportunity is real — but so is the uncertainty. Nokia was entering a market where Arista had built dominant data centre switching position, Cisco held enormous routing incumbency, Juniper-HPE brought its own ambitions, and NVIDIA's Spectrum-X competed for GPU cluster interconnect budget. Hyperscaler procurement is faster-moving and more technically demanding than carrier markets; a single Microsoft engagement does not constitute a business line.

## Huawei: Restrictions That Could Narrow or Reverse

The geopolitical dimension of Nokia's competitive environment was embodied most directly in Huawei. The Chinese vendor's exclusion from 5G deployments across the United Kingdom, Sweden, and several other European markets had benefited Nokia and Ericsson over the preceding four years — but that exclusion was never a permanent condition and was subject to shifting diplomatic currents between Brussels, Washington, and Beijing.

As of the frozen snapshot date of May 2026, Huawei remained restricted in core network functions across most Western markets, but the enforcement landscape had become more complicated. Some European operators had sought extensions to rip-and-replace timelines on cost grounds. Sovereign exemptions for certain network layers had been negotiated in specific jurisdictions. And in markets across Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and sub-Saharan Africa — where Nokia competed vigorously for carrier contracts — Huawei faced no restrictions at all and competed with the full weight of Chinese state-backed vendor financing behind it.

The risk ran in both directions. A material relaxation of Huawei restrictions in Europe would directly threaten Mobile Networks revenue. A tightening of restrictions in markets where Nokia currently competed on commercially neutral terms could provide upside — but could equally trigger retaliatory Chinese procurement policies that disadvantaged Nokia in markets where it had significant presence.

## Patent Licensing: High-Margin, High-Stakes Renewals

Nokia Technologies, the group's patent licensing arm, contributed revenue that was disproportionately profitable relative to its absolute size. The portfolio — built over decades of research investment in fundamental wireless communications standards — generated licensing income from handset manufacturers and other companies practising cellular standards globally. [Nokia Investor Relations](https://www.nokia.com/investors/)

The business model was structurally sound but periodically exposed to litigation and renewal risk. Major licensing agreements with large handset manufacturers were negotiated on multi-year cycles, and the renegotiation of any significant agreement carried the risk of either revenue reduction or costly arbitration. Nokia had navigated several such disputes historically, including prolonged litigation with Apple in the 2010s that ultimately resolved in Nokia's favour and produced a substantial licensing settlement.

The forward risk was that the composition of the handset industry continued to evolve in ways that complicated licensing. The rise of Chinese original equipment manufacturers — Xiaomi, Oppo, Vivo — as the dominant volume players in global smartphone shipments created counterparties with different negotiating postures and greater willingness to litigate in multiple jurisdictions simultaneously. Any significant gap in licensing coverage from a major manufacturer would fall directly to Nokia's bottom line.

## The Execution Challenge of the Hotard Succession

The execution challenge is that Nokia — a European telecom vendor with decades-deep carrier relationships — must develop new customer relationships and engineering credibilities in a market where it is not yet a known quantity. Transition risk extends to the leadership layer: any significant departure from the executive team carrying carrier relationship capital would set back commercial execution even as strategy shifts.

chapters.title: Hotard era execution, Infinera integration, AI data centre routing
chapters.body:
## The Intel alumnus inherits a compressed revenue line

Justin Hotard became CEO on April 1, 2025, with a task not merely to arrest the revenue decline from the €24.9 billion 2022 peak but to develop a new growth vector: positioning Nokia as infrastructure supplier to the AI hyperscale build-out.

## Infinera integration and the optical networks expansion

The Infinera close (February 28, 2025) gave Nokia hyperscaler relationships its legacy equipment business had never cultivated. Analysts at [Light Reading](https://www.lightreading.com) noted the deal provided a sales motion inside AWS, Google, and Meta. Integration execution over the twelve months following close would determine whether that relationship capital translates into contracted revenue.

## SR Linux and the AI data centre routing opportunity

SR Linux — the container-native network OS detailed in the IP & R&D chapter — is the instrument through which Nokia articulates its AI data centre routing ambition. Nokia's argument is that SR Linux combined with the Infinera optical layer offers hyperscalers a single-vendor solution across Layer 0-through-3. The differentiation is optical integration depth and carrier-grade reliability inherited from Bell Labs.

## Revenue trajectory and the recovery thesis

Hotard's recovery thesis rests on a different revenue mix: AI data centre infrastructure as a faster-growing segment, combined with Nokia Technologies' high-margin patent licensing baseline insulated from carrier capex cyclicality.

## Competitive position and the peer set

In AI data centre routing, the threats come from Cisco, Juniper, Arista, and (outside Western channels) Huawei — not Ericsson. Nokia's differentiation is the optical capability that can be bundled into the same hyperscaler conversation as IP routing — spanning WDM capacity to the routed IP layer.

## Execution risk acknowledged

Nokia was pitching against Arista at scale while simultaneously integrating a large acquisition and installing a new chief executive. The execution risk was acknowledged in the analyst community. What Nokia possessed that Arista did not was the Alcatel-Lucent deep routing heritage and, after February 2025, a material optical capability that could be bundled into the same hyperscaler conversation.

## Strategic posture, 2026–2030

As of the frozen snapshot in May 2026, the Hotard era was approximately thirteen months old. The broad outlines of the strategic posture had been communicated, but the financial results that would validate or refute them remained, in large measure, ahead of Nokia. The integration of Infinera was the most immediate operational variable: delivering cost synergies, retaining design engineering talent concentrated at Infinera's San Jose and Allentown facilities, and converting hyperscaler access into contracted volume would define the Network Infrastructure segment's trajectory through the remainder of the decade.

Nokia's structural advantage was the breadth of portfolio — optical, routing, radio and software — assembled over thirty years of acquisitions stretching from the 1992 purchase of Technophone through to the Infinera close. Hotard's task was to make that breadth coherent to a set of customers, the AI hyperscalers, who had historically sourced each layer of their network from best-of-breed specialists. Whether Nokia could shift that procurement logic in its favour — and do so while managing the Mobile Networks decline through a still-uncertain carrier capex recovery — remained the central question of the era he had inherited from Espoo's fifth floor.

The composition reflects the company's multi-business-group positioning across telecommunications, network infrastructure, mobile networks, cloud and network services, and patent licensing categories. The Baldauf Chair role plus the Hook telecommunications-CEO experience plus the Kozel Cisco-Systems-senior-leadership experience are the most strategically calibrated single director choices for the broader telecommunications-customer-category-relevant board governance.
